title: Metrology of quantum imaging schemes
abstract: We compare the performance of quantum imaging schemes based on spatially correlated photon pairs by formulating them as quantum multiparameter estimation problems, in which the object is characterized by transmission coefficients associated with different spatial modes. Our work focuses on standard quantum imaging techniques such as ghost imaging, two-photon imaging, and imaging with undetected photons. Specifically, we compute the quantum Fisher information matrices and show that they are saturated by Fisher information matrices corresponding to measurements in the object-mode basis, which generalize the common detection schemes employed in each imaging configuration. We find that ghost imaging and two-photon imaging generally provide higher precision for transmission estimation than imaging with undetected photons, but the latter is the only one that naturally does not couple transmission estimation across different spatial modes. These results identify which imaging protocols are best suited for specific tasks and provide practical guidelines for the design and optimization of quantum sensing technologies based on spatial correlations.
summary: This paper theoretically compares three quantum imaging techniques—Ghost Imaging, Two-Photon Imaging, and Undetected Photon Imaging—for estimating an object's transmission profile. By calculating Quantum Fisher Information matrices, the authors determine that while GI and TP are generally more precise, UP offers the unique advantage of allowing independent estimation for each spatial mode. The work provides practical guidelines for designing quantum sensing technologies based on photon correlations.
main_problem: The paper compares the ultimate quantum precision limits for estimating multiple unknown transmission coefficients ($\{	au_k\}$) characterizing an object using different quantum imaging schemes.
main_result: While Ghost Imaging and Two-Photon Imaging generally offer higher precision than imaging with undetected photons, the latter is unique in allowing independent estimation of each spatial mode's transmission coefficient.
method: The authors formulate the problem as a quantum multiparameter estimation task, calculating and comparing Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrices derived from various measurement protocols.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum imaging using spatially correlated photon pairs generated via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC). The object's transmission is modeled by unknown coefficients ($	au_k$) acting on the probe state.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information matrices ($F$ and $Q$), achievable variances ($\sigma(	au)$), and the comparison between Ghost Imaging (GI), Two-Photon Imaging (TP), and Undetected Photon Imaging (UP).
important_parameters: Object transmission coefficients ($	au_k$), Schmidt number ($K$), and the spatial correlation properties of the photon pairs.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the singular-mode basis characterizing the object structure is known beforehand; furthermore, some analyses simplify by assuming the object basis matches the signal Schmidt basis.
figures_summary: Figure 3 plots variances ($\sigma_{kk}$) for GI, TP, and UP as functions of transmission $	au_k$, showing a comparative performance landscape across different schemes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops quantum metrology tools (QFI/QCRB) to analyze three distinct imaging protocols (GI, TP, UP), deriving the optimal measurement settings for each case and comparing their resulting precision limits.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for optimizing quantum sensing in optical systems by quantifying the fundamental limits imposed by quantum correlations, which is highly relevant to advanced quantum optics research.
